title: Issue management approach, issue register, issue report and principles
blurb: Explain the purpose of the three issues products, who does what with issues, and how the practice supports the principles.
question: Project support needs to know how changes to approved products will be assessed and controlled. Which product should they read, and how does it differ from the issue register?

teach.h: Three products support the issues practice
teach.body: The issue management approach, held in the PID, describes how issues will be captured and reported and how changes to the project baseline will be assessed and controlled. The issue register, in the project log, captures and maintains information on all formal issues. The issue report describes an issue's impact on the baseline, identifies ways to resolve it or address an off-specification, and recommends a decision.

head: Product
Lives in
Purpose in a phrase
rows: How issues and baseline changes are handled
Impact, options and a recommended decision

teach.body: Developed in initiating a project, the issue management approach is the procedure, not the list. It typically covers configuration and version control, the scales for rating priority and severity, the delegated change authority and how the change budget is used. It replaced the 6th edition change control approach, is approved by the board as part of the PID, and is reviewed at stage boundaries.

The issue register is set up in initiating a project and records each formal issue, including its issue owner. An issue is closed once it has been considered and any change implemented; at each stage boundary the register is reviewed to close stage issues and add next-stage ones. The issue report is prepared by the project manager when an issue needs formal review. Within tolerance, it is an issue report, not an exception report.

head: Role
Area of focus
rows: Ultimate authority for changes; may delegate
Manages issue and change control procedures
Implements corrective actions in the work package
teach.caption: With no project support, the project manager maintains the issue register (manual tab 10.2).

teach.body: Each formal issue has an issue owner, the person who makes sure that particular issue is managed and resolved. The project manager runs the issue and change control procedures for the whole project, assisted by project support where possible, and implements corrective actions, for example by preparing product descriptions and work packages for agreed extra scope.

teach.h: How the issues practice supports the principles
head: Principle
Link
rows: Weigh a change's benefit against its cost and risk
Delegated change authority; escalate beyond limits
Baselines and product versions under change control
Delegation and register reviewed at stage boundaries
Change authority and issue roles agreed and documented
Formality of issue control fits the project
Issues can be a source of lessons
teach.caption: A study summary; the manual's tab 10.3 gives the official wording.

teach.body: Pennine Valley Rail is making six stations step-free. In initiation, project manager Joseph Okafor writes the issue management approach: a five-point severity scale, a change authority led by senior user Farah Iqbal, and a £40,000 change budget. Project support officer Amy Liu maintains the issue register. When a lift supplier goes into administration, station manager Brian Hollis is named issue owner, and Joseph prepares an issue report recommending a second supplier.

teach.text: Classic traps: the issue management approach holds the procedure; the issue register holds the actual issues. The issue owner looks after one issue; the project manager runs the procedures. And the issue management approach is NOT the change management approach, which covers organizational transition.

items: Issue management approach (PID): how issues are captured and reported and how baseline changes are assessed and controlled.
Issue register (project log): captures and maintains formal issues, each with an issue owner.
Issue report: impact on the baseline, ways to resolve, recommended decision.
PM manages the procedures; project support maintains the register; team managers implement corrective actions; the senior user decides escalated issues with a focus on benefits.
Links: business justification, manage by exception, focus on products, manage by stages, roles, tailoring, learning.

summary: You can now explain the purpose of the issue management approach, the issue register and the issue report, and who does what with issues. You can also link the issues practice to the principles, such as manage by exception through delegated change authority.

A.q: What is the purpose of the issue management approach?
options: To describe how risks are managed, with procedures, scales and roles
To describe how the organization will move to its target state
To describe the quality techniques, standards and responsibilities
To describe how issues are handled and baseline changes controlled
A.why: The issue management approach describes how issues will be captured and reported and how changes to the project baseline will be assessed and controlled (manual 10.5).

whyNot.0: That is the risk management approach.
whyNot.1: That is the change management approach.
whyNot.2: That is the quality management approach.

A.q: Which management product captures and maintains information on all formal issues?
A.why: The issue register, part of the project log, captures and maintains information on all formal issues.

whyNot.0: An issue report describes one issue needing formal review and recommends a decision.
whyNot.2: The daily log holds informal and sensitive issues.
whyNot.3: The approach describes the procedure; it does not hold the issues themselves.

A.q: Which product identifies ways to resolve an issue or address an off-specification and recommends a decision?
A.why: The issue report describes the issue's impact on the baseline, identifies ways to resolve it and recommends a decision.

whyNot.0: The issue register records formal issues but does not set out options and a recommendation for one.
whyNot.1: An exception report is for a forecast breach of stage or project tolerance.
whyNot.3: The daily log is the PM's informal diary.

B.q:
Which two statements about issue roles are correct?
1. Project support administers the issue procedures by maintaining the issue register.
2. The team manager manages the issue and change control procedures for the project.
3. The project manager implements corrective actions, such as work packages for agreed extra scope.
4. The issue owner runs the issue and change control procedures for the project.
B.why: Project support maintains the issue register (1), and the project manager implements corrective actions such as new work packages (3).

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is false: the project manager manages the issue and change control procedures.
whyNot.1: Both are false: the project manager runs the procedures, and the issue owner looks after one issue.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is false: the issue owner manages a single issue; the PM runs the procedures.

B.q: A small project has no project support. Who should maintain the issue register?
B.why: Project support normally maintains the issue register; where a project has no project support, the project manager maintains it (manual tab 10.2).

whyNot.1: Team managers implement corrective actions in work packages; they do not maintain the issue register.
whyNot.2: The senior user decides escalated issues; register maintenance is a managing-level task.
whyNot.3: Project assurance is independent of the project manager and does not do project support work.

B.q: Which statement about the issue owner is correct?
options: The issue owner manages one issue; the PM runs the procedures
The issue owner runs the change control procedure for the project
The issue owner writes the project's issue management approach
The issue owner approves changes from the change budget
B.why: The issue owner makes sure one particular issue is managed and resolved; the project manager runs the issue and change control procedures.

whyNot.1: The project manager runs the procedures, assisted by project support.
whyNot.2: The project manager develops the issue management approach during initiation; the issue owner looks after one issue.
whyNot.3: Approving changes is for the board or a delegated change authority, not the issue owner as such.

C.q: The senior user is deciding on an escalated issue. What should be their particular focus, and where is the issue formally recorded?
options: Supplier and technical integrity; the issue register
Safeguarding the expected benefits; the daily log
Securing funding for the project; the issue report
Safeguarding the expected benefits; the issue register
C.why: The senior user decides escalated issues with particular focus on safeguarding the expected benefits, and formal issues are recorded in the issue register.

whyNot.0: Supplier and technical integrity is not the senior user's focus; the senior user represents users and benefits.
whyNot.1: The focus is right, but an escalated issue is formal, so it belongs in the issue register.
whyNot.2: Securing funding is the executive's responsibility, and the issue report is a report, not the record of issues.

C.q: The board delegates change authority within limits, and anything beyond those limits is escalated. Which principle does this support?
C.why: Delegating authority within defined limits and escalating beyond them is manage by exception.

whyNot.0: Manage by stages is about stage-by-stage planning and decision points, not limits of delegated authority.
whyNot.2: Focus on products is about defining and delivering products; the limits of authority are manage by exception.
whyNot.3: Learn from experience is about seeking and applying lessons.

C.q: A request for change is assessed by weighing its extra benefit against its extra cost and risk. Which principle is being applied?
C.why: What the project delivers must stay consistent with its justification, so a change's extra benefit is weighed against its extra cost and risk.

whyNot.1: Tailoring adapts the method to the project; it is not about justifying a change.
whyNot.2: Defining roles sets out who does what; it does not weigh benefits against costs.
whyNot.3: Learning from experience applies lessons; it is not the basis for weighing a change's value.

reteach.title: The hospital ward
reteach.question: How is a ward's complaints procedure different from its complaints file?

blocks.body: A hospital ward has a complaints procedure (how complaints are logged, graded and decided), a complaints file (every complaint received, each with a named handler) and, for a serious complaint, a written report setting out what happened, the options and a recommendation. The ward manager runs the procedure; each named handler looks after one complaint.

blocks.text: The approach is the rulebook; the register is the file of actual issues.

explain.body: The issue management approach is one of the management approaches held in the project initiation documentation, developed during initiating a project.

test.q: Where is the issue management approach held?
test.why: The issue management approach is part of the project initiation documentation.

whyNot.0: The project log holds the issue register, not the approach.
whyNot.1: The project brief is produced earlier, in starting up a project.
whyNot.3: A stage plan covers one stage's work; the approach applies across the project.

explain.body: The issue management approach typically sets out configuration and version control, priority and severity scales, the delegated change authority and how the change budget is used.

test.q: Project support needs the scales for rating issue severity and priority. Which product should they consult?
test.why: The issue management approach includes the priority and severity scales used to rate issues.

whyNot.0: The register records each issue's rating but does not define the scales.
whyNot.1: The risk management approach sets the scales for assessing risks, not issues.
whyNot.2: The quality management approach covers quality techniques, standards and responsibilities.

explain.body: The team manager implements corrective actions within the work package; the project manager implements them at the managing level, for example by issuing new or amended work packages.

test.q: Which role implements corrective actions within a work package?
test.why: The team manager implements corrective actions within the work package.

whyNot.0: Project support maintains the issue register.
whyNot.2: Project assurance advises the board and stays independent of delivery.
whyNot.3: The senior user decides escalated issues with a focus on benefits.

explain.body: Focus on products underpins planning, quality, scope and change control. Baselines and product versions are how the issues practice applies it.

test.q: Keeping baselines and product versions under change control links the issues practice most directly to which principle?
test.why: Product focus is the basis of scope and change control, so controlling baselined products applies focus on products.

whyNot.1: Manage by stages is about stage-by-stage planning and decision points.
whyNot.2: Tailoring adapts the method, including how formal issue control is; it is not about controlling product versions.
whyNot.3: Learn from experience is about lessons.
